summary: Option B: phased. The only forced change is the capacity: P1 retires in December, so move the existing models to F64 first, unchanged. That is cheap, low-risk and reversible. Then, as a second phase with its own business case, mirror NorthwindDW into OneLake, build gold tables with T-SQL in a Fabric Warehouse (the team's skill), and move the Sales model to Direct Lake on OneLake with security in the semantic model. Finance stays Import (small, daily, strict access), and Ops moves off DirectQuery to the mirrored data to remove the WMS load. Revisit if capacity use passes 80% or the mirror lags more than 15 minutes.
root_cause: Forced: Premium per-capacity (P SKU) retirement at renewal in December. Optional: everything beyond lift and shift.
Latency needs differ by workload: Ops 15 minutes; Sales 4 hours; Finance daily after close; Web daily. "Real time for everything" is one workload's requirement presented as everyone's.
The binding constraints are skills (SQL yes, Spark no), budget (flat), security (Finance access must not weaken) and source load (DirectQuery on the WMS causes 9am spikes).
steps: Phase 1 (Sep–Nov): assign the workspaces to an F64 capacity and keep the models as they are. Measure capacity units (CU) for a month. Rollback: the P1 stays until December.
Phase 2a (Q1): mirror NorthwindDW into OneLake (SQL Server 2016+ via the gateway, CDC). Replication compute is free; queries use the capacity.
Phase 2b: build gold star-schema tables in a Fabric Warehouse with T-SQL (no Spark needed) as materialised tables, not views, because Direct Lake on OneLake can't use non-materialised views.

Phase 2c: rebuild Sales as Direct Lake on OneLake over the gold tables. Keep RLS in the semantic model (SQL-endpoint RLS would not apply in OneLake mode). Refresh becomes framing: seconds instead of 74 minutes.

Ops: point the fulfilment model at the mirrored WMS data in OneLake instead of DirectQuery against the WMS. It meets 15 minutes (mirroring lag permitting) and removes the 9am CPU spikes. Validate the lag first.
Finance stays Import: 6.4M rows, daily, strict access. Moving it buys nothing and risks the control Sarah cares about.

Budget: F64 replaces P1 (no increase); mirroring storage and compute are included up to the capacity's limits; the business case for Phase 2 is the removed refresh window, the WMS load and the retired nightly ETL.
Record the decision with a revisit trigger, and refer back to it in the next architecture review (Sprint 10).

artifacts.title: ADR-009 (model answer)
body: **ADR-009: Target analytics architecture for 2027.** Status: proposed, 23 Jul 2026.

**Context:** P1 capacity retires at renewal (Dec 2026); F64 is the equivalent. Sales model 182M rows, refresh 74 min and rising ~3 min/month; Ops uses DirectQuery on the WMS (CPU 83% peaks); team skilled in SQL and DAX, not Spark; flat budget.
**Options:** A lift and shift; B phased (F64 now, then mirroring + Warehouse gold + Direct Lake on OneLake for Sales and Ops); C big-bang Lakehouse/Spark; D DirectQuery everywhere.

**Consequences:** Phase 1 changes nothing for users. Phase 2 removes the Sales refresh window and the WMS load; gold logic moves from Power Query to T-SQL in the Warehouse; RLS stays in the semantic model; Finance remains Import.

**Risks:** CU usage exceeds F64 (monitor with the Capacity Metrics app; mitigate by scheduling and optimising before scaling up). Mirroring lag too high for Ops (validate in a pilot; keep DirectQuery as fallback until proven). Direct Lake guardrails as data grows (keep Delta tables optimised).
**Revisit if:** CU > 80% sustained for two weeks, mirror lag > 15 min at peak, or Sales refresh/framing fails more than twice a month.

options.a: Safe and on time, and the right Phase 1, but as the whole decision it leaves the 74-minute refresh growing and the WMS load in place. You'll be back here in a year with less time.
options.b: This is the model answer: it separates the forced change from the optional one, uses the team's skills, keeps Finance's controls and removes the two real pains, with a rollback at every step.
options.c: Technically capable but fails the skills and budget constraints and puts the December deadline at risk. A big bang also makes rollback very hard.
options.d: Gives freshness nobody but Ops needs, moves the load problem to every source system, and makes every report as slow as its source. It's the opposite of what the evidence asks for.

communication.executive: We have to change our Power BI capacity by December, and we'll do that first at the same cost, with nothing changing for users. Then we propose a second step: copy the warehouse into Fabric continuously, so sales data is ready in seconds instead of over an hour each night and the warehouse system stops slowing down at 9am. Finance's reports stay as they are. Each step can be undone. We'll come back with the numbers before committing to step two.
communication.engineer: Phase 1: workspaces to F64, no model changes, baseline CU. Phase 2: mirror NorthwindDW (CDC via gateway) → Warehouse gold tables in T-SQL (materialised, no views) → Sales as Direct Lake on OneLake with semantic-model RLS; Ops repointed from DQ-on-WMS to mirrored tables; Finance stays Import. Revisit at CU > 80%, lag > 15 min.

pitfalls: Treating "move to Fabric" as one decision. The capacity change is forced; the architecture change isn't.
Building Direct Lake on OneLake over SQL views: not supported. Materialise them.
Keeping RLS in the SQL endpoint while using Direct Lake on OneLake: it isn't applied there. Put RLS in the semantic model.
Choosing Spark notebooks for a team without Spark skills and a December deadline.
Promising "real time" without asking who needs it and for which decision.

review.junior: Recommends the newest option (Lakehouse + Direct Lake everywhere) because it's the future.
review.competent: Compares options against features and picks a sensible target, but as one big step.
review.senior: Quantifies the latency needs, respects the team's skills and the budget, knows the Direct Lake rules (views, RLS, fallback) and phases the change with rollbacks.
review.architect: Separates forced from optional, writes the ADR with a revisit trigger, ties phase 2 to a business case the CFO can defend, and makes the decision referenceable in later reviews.
